concern: In 2019 PepsiCo sued nine Gujarat farmers over alleged intellectual-property infringement involving potato seed, then withdrew all the suits. In 2024 the New York Times reported debt, child marriage and hysterectomies among sugar cane cutters in Maharashtra, in a sugar supply chain linked to PepsiCo and Coca-Cola. PepsiCo called the description deeply concerning and said it would assess conditions with its partners. In the Break Free From Plastic brand audits, volunteers in 42 countries found PepsiCo among the three most frequently found brands in plastic waste, after Coca-Cola. The audit says it shows common brands in cleanups, not exact amounts of pollution.
source: Moneylife; Business and Human Rights Resource Centre (summary of the New York Times report); Down To Earth, reporting Break Free From Plastic

concern: A report by Public Eye and IBFAN, with samples tested in a Belgian lab, said Cerelac baby cereals sold in India contain added sugar, nearly 3 g per serving on average. Nestlé India said it had cut added sugars in its infant cereals by up to 30% over five years. In 2015 India's food regulator banned Maggi noodles over lead above permitted limits; the Bombay High Court lifted the ban in August 2015 and ordered fresh tests, and Nestlé said all 90 retested samples were within limits. Separately, a US Supreme Court case (Nestlé USA v. Doe) was brought by six Malian adults who said they were trafficked as children to work on Ivorian cocoa farms; in 2021 the court dismissed it on jurisdiction grounds, not on the facts.
source: Business Today, reporting Public Eye and IBFAN; Business Today; PBS NewsHour

concern: The Uttar Pradesh Pollution Control Board ordered the closure of Coca-Cola's bottling plant at Mehdiganj, Varanasi, citing excessive groundwater extraction and effluents above permissible limits. The company has denied the allegations and appealed to the National Green Tribunal. At Plachimada in Kerala, villagers said the bottling plant (opened 2000) drained local wells; the panchayat cancelled its licence in 2003 and the plant closed in 2004. A Kerala expert committee set compensation at Rs 216 crore, which the company has not paid; Coca-Cola India says independent studies did not support the allegations. Coca-Cola was also the most frequently found brand in Break Free From Plastic's 2018 audits across 42 countries.
source: Eco-Business; HuffPost India; Down To Earth

concern: Workers at Hindustan Unilever's thermometer factory in Kodaikanal, Tamil Nadu, said they were poisoned by mercury. The factory was shut in 2001 after about 7.4 tonnes of mercury-laced glass waste was found, and workers campaigned for about 15 years. In March 2016 the company settled with the workers on undisclosed terms. Worker groups estimated deaths and illnesses; these figures are their estimates, not court findings.

In 2014 The Guardian published a documentary on the Narahani tea estate in Assam, run by Amalgamated Plantations, in which Tata Global Beverages held about 41%. It reported pickers paid about half the minimum wage and girls lured away by traffickers. Tata said the estate does not supply its Tetley brand, said wages follow an industry-wide agreement, instructed defamation lawyers and promised an independent audit.
In December 2021, after about two months of a strike by union workers at its US cereal plants, Kellogg announced it would hire permanent replacements for the strikers.

ITC is India's leading cigarette maker; cigarettes were 62% of gross revenue in 2016, and BAT held about a quarter of ITC in 2024. Researchers and media have criticised its cigarette promotion despite India's advertising ban, and it has joined litigation against larger pictorial health warnings, shutting its cigarette factories in protest in 2010 and 2016.

A US-government-funded study found about 1.56 million children working in cocoa production in Ghana and Ivory Coast, and the share of cocoa-area children in child labour rose from 31% (2008/09) to 45% (2018/19). It named Mars, Hershey, Nestlé and Cargill, whose industry had pledged in 2010 to cut the worst child labour by 70% by 2020. Mars said it committed $1 billion to responsible sourcing.

The Thrissur District Consumer Commission found that Nutri Choice Thin Arrowroot biscuit packs labelled 300 g weighed about 268 g and 249 g, called it an unfair trade practice, and ordered Rs 50,000 compensation plus costs. The report says Britannia did not appear in the proceedings.
source: SCC Online (Thrissur Consumer Commission order dated 26 Sept 2023)

concern: The US FDA rejected 53 Haldiram's export consignments in a month, citing suspected pesticide presence and products not adequately processed or packed in unsanitary conditions. Haldiram's said its food is completely safe.

In June 2019 a district task force raided a biscuit factory in Raipur and rescued 26 children aged 12 to 16. Parle said none of its factories employ anyone under 18 and that this factory is run by a third-party subcontractor, not by Parle.

In December 2020 the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) reported that, in NMR tests run by a German laboratory, only three of 13 honey brands passed, and that Dabur, Patanjali, Baidyanath, Zandu, Hitkari and Apis Himalaya failed, which CSE said indicated added sugar syrup. Dabur called the findings "motivated and aimed at maligning our brand", said its honey is 100 per cent pure, and shared a German NMR report saying its honey passed.
source: The Week, reporting the Centre for Science and Environment

concern: In December 2020 the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) reported that Patanjali honey failed an NMR purity test run by a German laboratory, which CSE said indicated added sugar syrup; Patanjali and Dabur both questioned the study. Separately, the Supreme Court heard a plea by the Indian Medical Association accusing Patanjali Ayurveda of misleading advertisements about modern medicine. In February 2024 it issued a contempt notice to the company and its managing director, and on 2 April 2024 it refused to accept their apology, calling it "perfunctory". The court case concerns medicine advertising, not food.

In October 2003 Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration said it found insects in Cadbury Dairy Milk chocolates and ordered a statewide seizure. Cadbury denied any infestation, blamed poor storage at retail outlets, and said its samples from the Bombay factory were free of infestation.

In 2014 the Delaware Court of Chancery declined to dismiss a case in which a Hershey shareholder, the Louisiana Municipal Police Employees' Retirement System, accused the company of complicity in child labour and trafficking on West African cocoa farms, and sought to inspect its books. Hershey said the court had found no wrongdoing and would defend against an "overly-broad and unmerited effort". A 2020 US-government-funded study also named Hershey among the companies whose cocoa areas saw child labour rise (31% to 45% of children between 2008/09 and 2018/19).

In June 2015 Uttar Pradesh's food regulator said one sampled Mother Dairy milk packet failed tests, reporting detergent and fat levels below the claimed amount. Mother Dairy denied it, saying the sample was loose village-level milk drawn before it reached the chilling centre and had been sent for retesting.

On 1 July 2015, during the Maggi noodle row, Indo Nissin withdrew Top Ramen from the Indian market at the food regulator's request, because the product's approval was still pending. The company said Top Ramen had been sold in India since 1991 with no safety issue or recall.

In June 2024 a Noida customer said she found a centipede in an Amul ice cream tub bought through a delivery app. Noida's food safety department opened a probe. Amul expressed regret and asked for the tub to investigate, but said the customer declined to hand it over, so it could not comment on the specific issue. No finding against the company is reported.

On 19 June 2024 a Jamnagar resident complained of a dead frog in a packet of Balaji Crunchex wafers. The municipal corporation ordered an inquiry, and a preliminary probe by a food safety officer indicated it was a decomposed frog; samples from the batch were to be collected. The complainant said the distributor and customer care gave no satisfactory reply. The report carries no statement from Balaji.

In July 2026 FSSAI issued a notice to Heritage Foods asking why action should not be taken, saying its "Fresh Paneer" claim does not meet the conditions for using the word "Fresh" and that "Healthy Happiness" may not conform to the claims rules. The notice followed consumer complaints and FSSAI's own review; the report carries no response from the company.

In June 2026 FSSAI issued a notice to Marico over its Saffola Total Heart Pro cooking oil, saying the "Heart Pro" wording and heart images could lead consumers to expect heart-health benefits beyond approved claims, and that claims such as "Good Fats Balance" and "Losorb for less oil absorption" need scientific support.
source: Agron Food Processing, reporting FSSAI notices

concern: In November 2024 the Delhi High Court granted Marico (maker of Saffola oats) an interim order, issued before Alpino was heard, barring Alpino Health Foods from running ads that disparage oats as a food category and directing Google to block the videos. This was an early-stage order, not a final judgement.
